title: How to Be Happy (in 3 Easy Steps)
credit: A photo essay. Original photos by Michael Kilcoyne.
description: Make a decision. Learn to live with the consequences. Don't question it. A photo essay on Denver, New York, and a year in Kyoto.

chapters.label: The Rules
blocks: How to be happy.
1. Make a decision.
2. Learn to accept and live with the consequences of that.
3. Don't question it.
In 2019, I was on the phone with a good friend when I told her, “I want to move to Japan.”
I didn't know why I wanted to move to Japan — after all, I'd spent some time there, I loved it, but I also loved my life in Denver.
But I just did. It felt like a decision that my soul had made, and my rational-mind had nothing to do with it.
When I told her that, it felt right.

And then, a few days later, I flew back home to Denver where I lived at the time, and as I was sitting in the Lyft back to my apartment, I just thought to myself, “This feels right, and I still can't explain why but it feels like my life here is finished.”

chapters.label: The Panic
blocks: Now, that was in April of 2019 — over the course of the next few months, I essentially started to work myself into a panic around my decision.
The notion of leaving a great circle of friends behind; a business that was just starting to get off the ground; and eventually someone who I could see myself being with, well.
It was brutal.

And I remember torturing myself over it — crying on the phone to friends; crying inside phone booths and rooms intended for pregnant women in coworking spaces; feeling absolutely panicked about my decision.
It was torturous, and I can tell you that those last few months of 2019 were some of the hardest months in my life.

chapters.heading: The Two Arrows
chapters.label: The Two Arrows
blocks: A friend of mine shared with me this brilliant parable that I still think about to this day.
He asked, “Have you heard of the tale of the two arrows?”
“No, I haven't,” I told him.
“Well, dude, you're doing the thing with two arrows — arrow number one is making the decision.”
“Uh-uh.”
“Arrow number two is questioning the decision. Don't hit yourself with arrow #2.”
I started to cry — I was already in an incredibly emotional place, and that just walloped me.
I'd started at Step 1, skipped straight-ahead to Step 3, and never really reckoned with Step 2 until it was too late, honestly.
That's a recipe for misery — that fight against ourselves.
Hitting yourself with Arrow #2.

chapters.heading: Making a Decision to Be Happy
chapters.label: A Decision
blocks: When I was working a miserable job in sales in 2013–2014 in New York City, I remember at one point reminding myself, “I'm tired of being miserable. This isn't fun anymore.”
I was either going to throw myself off my balcony, or learn to approach my role and my life a little differently, so I did.
Every morning, I'd wake up and reflect on things that I loved — “I love my family; I love my mom and dad; I love my job; I love my apartment,” etc.

When I ran out of things to love, I'd just look around my room and point at my mattress on the floor — it remained there for the entirety of my time there — and say, “I love my mattress on the floor.”
This was a thing I'd learned from a mentor of mine, Dave Kerpen, who would frequently espouse the benefits of gratitude.
It seemed to work for him. He had a bi-polar dad; his own experiences with manic depression.
But even in the midst of chaos in a big city like New York, he seemed to often be happy.
Gratitude and fear and anxiety and panic cannot live together at the same time.
So, for those few moments at least, when I'd reflect on my love for things, things started to change.

chapters.label: A Magnet
blocks: I was recently with a friend and she told me how, “New York is a magnet for feelings — if you're feeling like s**t, it'll magnetize more of that; good? That. It's a magnet.”
And I know that's true of life and perception, too — the more you reflect on negativity and fear and panic, the more you will see instances that will create more and more of that in your life.
Happiness starts with, above all things, a decision to be happy.*

* It's worth mentioning, here, that certain chemical and life-circumstances can often make this extremely challenging. If you're poor, your parents abuse you, and you're surrounded by violence, naturally, you'll find yourself in a state of survival. Gratitude can go so far, but extracting yourself from that environment any way you can and finding positive influences in the form of mentors or other relationships are equally as important, too.

chapters.heading: Learning to Live With the Consequences of It
chapters.label: The Consequences
blocks: I made the decision to leave New York City in 2014 and move to Denver — I'd only lived there for a year after college and, even though I grew up outside of the city and had always adored it, I knew that it wouldn't be the place for me in the long-term.

So I left — in a lot of ways, that decision probably drove my girlfriend at the time away (not to mention my complete inability to communicate my feelings and fears and all that); I left behind a close group of friends who'd slowly become acclimated to my weekly ‘Steaknight' ventures; and I quit a lucrative job in sales that I'd probably still be pursuing had I not.
The consequences were brutal — in the first year, I can probably count on one hand the number of new friends I'd made while living in Denver.
Mostly, I sat at home and wrote, worked the different sales jobs I'd picked up (and inevitably quit), and got drunk with my roommate in order to quell my insatiable anxiety.
I lost a lot of weight, too — life in New York meant a lot of drinking and a lot of going out to eat, and doing neither of those things helped me quickly shave off a few dozen pounds.
The first thing people would comment on is, “You look good!”
That was probably my first indication that this wasn't entirely a bad idea, but I couldn't help but wonder if it was.

chapters.label: Building Something
blocks: Ultimately, after a few more years of living there, finding a different roommate, and eventually building a great community of entrepreneurs and friends and awesome people through different meetups that I hosted or dinners (like Steaknight), I was able to build relationships and that made me feel less isolated and ultimately it did turn out to be, “A good decision,” but it wasn't until I'd beaten myself up for a year or two that I ultimately came to that conclusion.
There's something to be said about trusting your gut — after all, those decisions are generally quite accurate — but it can be impossibly difficult at times.
Especially when it's painful, which social isolation often is.

And, so, we tend to avoid experiencing those forms of pain, either by giving into it and falling back on our plan — which is OK, especially if it's not the right fit, as was the case when I lived in Los Angeles — or by self-medicating through alcohol, drugs, sex, or whatever form of self-medication we prefer (I've tried all of them).

Those consequences feel damning the more we're able to connect with the why behind our decision — why we left a certain work environment; why we decided to get into this relationship to begin with; why we stopped talking to that friend.

chapters.heading: Don't Question It
chapters.label: Don't Question It
blocks: Flash-forward to 2020.

A few months into living in Japan, I was hit with a whammy of bad, bad news — Covid had become a full-blown pandemic and the borders were essentially being shut down; my stock portfolio which I'd essentially relied upon for all of my self-worth (and financing my lifestyle) had cratered; and my dog, Tucker, had been put down by my parents.
It was like someone had sliced me open with a Katana and dumped a bunch of salt in there.
It was brutally painful.
Everything I saw was pain and scary and the only thing I could think was, “This is karma for moving in the first place.”
I had few friends — of my 15+ housemates, I probably got along with one person — and I was scared, and I was alone, and the 14+ hour time-difference didn't help.

chapters.label: The Kamogawa
blocks: So, when I could, I would run out to the Kamogawa river, which bisects the city of Kyoto — and I would go there and meditate and cry and reflect on love but mostly cry.
Kyoto is the most beautiful place for a soul to rest. I didn't see that at the beginning, but every time I revisit it, I'm reminded of just how tranquil it is.

And it was brutal, and I just kept thinking to myself, “Is this it? This is how this whole thing goes, huh…? It's just awful and shitty and then I leave, right…? I go back home, hat in hand, pride in tow?”
And honestly, I felt that way for a few months while I was there.

chapters.label: The Turn
blocks: Probably until April, when the weather started to get nicer and Japan started to open itself up. Covid apparently wasn't real there (yet).
One day, I was running around the city feeling utterly miserable and I just remember thinking to myself, “I can be miserable here. Or I can fall in love with living here, and make it work.”
And that was it — every morning, I started to think, “I'm going to love living here.”

So I stopped doing things that were making me miserable and having a negative impact on my day-to-day happiness and well-being — endlessly scrolling Reddit; dealing with difficult clients or bad business partners; worrying so God Damn much about my stock portfolio and detaching my self-worth from that; and refusing to really connect with my roommates in a meaningful way.
And I don't know if the environment shifted or I just found a community or what, but everything changed after that. It took a while, but it changed.

chapters.label: The Best Months
blocks: My time there was easily some of the most memorable months of my life — exploring the forests of Kyoto with roommates; night photography in Osaka with new friends; Steaknights at our long kitchen table; and dates along the Kamogawa river.
Just thinking to myself, “This is the best life ever. I am so lucky and fortunate and grateful to be able to do this.”

chapters.label: The Best Months
blocks: Shit, even the last few days there — eating snacks in a tiny hostel I'd rented for a few days with a few close friends before I'd ultimately leave Japan to go live in Turkey for a while — were some of the most memorable moments.
It was truly an extraordinary experience, because I let go.
I let go of trying to make it something that it would never become — a perfect cultural indoctrination into a place that I never really belonged in the first place.
It was just, “Let's make the best of this. And whatever happens, happens.”
And it did.

chapters.label: Letting Go
blocks: I started my career in filmmaking, in earnest, there.
I made lifelong friendships with people who I still keep in touch with to this day.
And I took some swings, creatively, that stretched me.
And looking back on it, I'm fond of my experiences and I barely even recall the challenging moments.
Because they felt so short-lived.

chapters.label: Letting Go
blocks: And, ultimately, I was happy not because everything in my life was amazing and awesome and perfect but, rather, because I spent more of my time and energy focusing on the things that were great.
And less time on the bullshit.

end.title: That's how to be happy.
end.shareSubject: A photo essay on how to be happy
